author: Lisa Xu
title: UFCW Members Protect Local Election After Sham Merger Attempt
content:
An insurgent slate is challenging the longtime incumbents in Local 8-Golden State, one of the largest locals in the United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW), in what may be the local’s first competitive election in decades. And now, after protecting the election from a sham merger attempt that would have canceled the election, the battle is on. 




Ballots are set to be mailed on November 21. But when members first saw the election notice in the local’s newsletter, they discovered a big “but.” The notice stated that the election would not proceed if Local 8 merged with another union, the 

Staffing Agencies Federated Employees

 (SAFE), before the end of the year. 




Members said they had never heard about this possible merger, or SAFE, before reading about it in the final sentence of the election notice, mailed to members on October 16. 




What is SAFE? Publicly available information about the organization, which has multiple ties to Local 8 President Jacques Loveall, raised more questions than answers. Neither Local 8, the UFCW International union, nor SAFE has responded to inquiries about the merger.




With the help of Essential Workers for Democracy, a UFCW reform organization focused on member education and union democracy, the insurgent slate urged the Department of Labor to investigate SAFE and the merger. After a federal investigator began to probe, the local told them the merger had been “postponed indefinitely.” 




A FAMILY AFFAIR







Local 8 represents 23,000 workers in grocery, meatpacking, health care, and cannabis across northern California and the Central Valley. End to end, it would take 10 hours to drive the length of the local’s jurisdiction. 




The reform slate 

At What Cost

 is running on opening up negotiations to members and training stewards in every workplace. Wages for grocery workers have stagnated across California. A 

2025 study

 sponsored by several other UFCW locals on understaffing at Kroger and Albertsons found a high degree of financial insecurity among their workers. 




“Grocery careers, once dignified, have been reduced to second jobs for most,” said Eric Marcuz, a veteran Safeway worker who is running for president on the At What Cost slate. The local has not had a competitive election in at least 40 years.




Marcuz’s slate created a 

page

 to try to provide members more information about the merger, and sent a 

letter of complaint

 to Local 8, UFCW International, and the Department of Labor over what they saw as an effort to avoid a democratic election. 




The At What Cost slate is running against a slate of incumbents—the 

Solidarity Works Team

— headed by Loveall, who has been president of Local 8 and its predecessor union, Local 588, since 2004. He took over the position from his father, 

Jack Loveall

, who became president of Local 588 in 1984, after working in high-level positions for the UFCW International and one of its predecessor unions, the Retail Clerks, for many years. 




When the elder Loveall retired, he was one of the highest-paid union officers in the country, earning more than $567,000 in compensation a year, equivalent to over a million dollars today. 




“The Loveall family has led our union for decades,” said Marcuz. “Over that time they have consolidated power at the top and completely distanced themselves from the workers they claim to represent. While their wealth and wages have ballooned, the members have been left behind.” 




On his LinkedIn page, the younger Loveall describes himself as “Chief Executive Officer of trade organization (UFCW8.org).” He received $306,000 in total compensation from the local last year, plus another $20,000 salary as an International Vice President and 

$34,752

 from his role as a trustee of the UFCW Vacation Compensation Trusts. Loveall is also the director and co-founder of Solidaritus, a for-profit health care company that Local 8 has purchased millions of dollars of shares in, as have other unions. 




‘THAT’S THEIR MODE OF OPERATING’




Leaders of the local have used a merger to avoid a competitive election before. In 2006, a slate of 

reformers

 planned a challenge to the leadership of then-Local 588, including Loveall. But prior to the scheduled election, Local 588 

merged

 with Local 1288 to form Local 8-Golden State, and elections were put off until 2008. 




Meanwhile, Doug Slaydon, a 25-year meat cutter and the reform slate’s candidate for union president, was 

fired

 from Safeway on the pretext of a customer complaint in 2006. The firing occurred a day after a 20-store campaign blitz by his slate, 588 Members for a Democratic Union.




“That's their mode of operating,” Slaydon said, referring to the mergers. “That's how they got around my attempt at an election.” 




“Federal law is clear: local unions must hold officer elections at least every three years,” said Will Bloom, a professor at the CUNY School of Law and a board member of the Association for Union Democracy. “Any attempt to forestall an election through a sham merger, in an effort to quash dissent and make member participation more difficult, goes against the basic principles of union democracy law.”




A REAL UNION?




The proposed merger with SAFE immediately raised the eyebrows of members and the Department of Labor. 




It is not clear who SAFE represents, or whether it is even a union. On its 

website

, SAFE calls itself a “labor-driven initiative committed to securing union inclusion and equitable treatment for workers employed through staffing agencies.” 




However, there are no union election filings by SAFE with the National Labor Relations Board, nor any other public documentation of where members are being organized. The organization’s website is filled with stock photos, rather than photos of actual members.




An initial 

LM-1 form

 for SAFE was filed on February 9, 2026 by Patricia Schreiter, who 

appears

 to be a 

relative

 of Loveall, and has no other public connection to the labor movement. Schreiter was not listed on SAFE’s website as an officer, although the LM-1 form lists her as president. After members and a federal investigator from the Department of Labor began asking questions, the page listing SAFE’s officers and staff was removed from its site. 




As of early last week, the SAFE homepage stated the organization was 

“9,800 Strong and Growing,”

 but this figure has since been removed. A legislative update on the SAFE site from September 30 included a 

reference

 to union mergers as a strategy “to build a larger, stronger, more unified organization,” as “bigger unions win bigger protections”, but this language has also been removed.




The SAFE website features dozens of articles about the SAFE Act, or SB 1032, a California state senate bill sponsored by Senator Eloise Reyes that would tighten regulatory standards for temporary staffing agencies and require them to buy workers’ compensation insurance. Loveall has been a vocal supporter of the bill via the UFCW Western States Council, the bill’s co-sponsor.




However, an aide for Senator Reyes told 

Labor Notes

 that the SAFE union was not registered as a group in support of the bill, or one that they had personally interacted with.




WEB OF CONNECTIONS




There are a number of suggestive ties between SAFE and an organization called 

The PACT

, which claims to be a 501(c)5 labor organization for temp workers. Until early last week SAFE’s organizing director was 

listed

 as Fernando Cisneros, whose LinkedIn 

profile

 states that he is also a full-time “Growth Leader” at The PACT. (Cisneros’s name disappeared when SAFE removed that section of its website.)




The PACT has an arrangement with a company called 

Samuel Hale

, which provides workers’ compensation insurance to the employers of temp workers and acts as a co-employer of those workers. 




“In addition to passing along savings to our customers, Samuel Hale also reinvests a percentage of every payroll dollar worked into a benefits fund managed by The PACT, a 501c5, exclusively focused on developing and administering new benefits to our growing 10,000+ member population,” Samuel Hale writes on its website. These workers appear to be mostly immigrant workers in sectors including warehouse work, food processing, and domestic services.




As of earlier this week, SAFE’s website had a section called 

“Health Care & Retirement Benefits,”

 which stated that SAFE members will receive a defined benefit pension plan, as well as comprehensive medical coverage. These are both benefits which 

The PACT claims to offer

 to its employees. This section on the SAFE website, too, has since been removed. 




Samuel Hale and Local 8 appear to have a collective bargaining agreement, and  seem to be utilizing California’s Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) carve-out, a state law that allows for workers’ compensation claims to be directly arbitrated between a union and employer, bypassing the state’s worker compensation board. A collective bargaining agreement must be in place in order to qualify for the carve-out.




Loveall of Local 8 (then Local 588) appears to have signed a 

collective bargaining agreement

 in 2005 with Samuel Hale on behalf of The Professional and Commercial Trades Association (PACT), according to a 

video

 posted on the company’s Facebook page. In a 

2025 workers’ comp appeal

 case, a Samuel Hale spokesperson said that the Samuel Hale employees are covered by a UFCW CBA and that The PACT is “a wing of the UFCW.” However, the details of this agreement are unclear and cannot be found online. The worker who filed the appeal also said that Local 8 was unable to provide “any information regarding alleged union membership,” even as Samuel Hale affirmed that union dues were being deducted from employee paychecks.




Samuel Hale says that it can help employers cut workers’ comp claim costs by up to 50 percent, and boasts that it is the only entity covered by the California ADR carve-out that can extend the carve-out’s protection to other employers, thanks to its CBA with Local 8.




In addition to the web of connections between SAFE, The PACT, Samuel Hale, and Local 8, SAFE’s 

articles of incorporation

 were filed July 17, 2025 by 

Ellen Anreder

. Anreder is the CEO of 

Bleiweiss Communications

, a major vendor for Local 8. Website 

metadata

 indicates that SAFE’s website was also created by Bleiweiss. 




Anreder and Loveall together serve on several non-profit boards that Local 8 has financial ties to, including 

CORPaTH

, the 

Food and Drug Conference

, the 

Loveall Foundation for Children

, and 

All Trusts Cooperative

 (of which Anreder and Loveall are the only two board members), with a collective net assets of over $10 million.




FUTURES AT STAKE




In the UFCW, local union bylaws typically allow for elections to be called at any point in a six-month window preceding the end of a term, giving incumbents a powerful advantage, since challengers can't be sure when exactly they might need to take time off to collect nomination signatures or campaign to turn out the vote. What’s more, Local 8 has scheduled ballots to be mailed during the week of Thanksgiving, a universal blackout period for time off in the grocery retail sector. That’s exactly the week when candidates could most effectively campaign at worksites.




The At What Cost slate notified the local union of their intent to run in August 2025, although reformers have been publicly agitating in the local since late 2024.




But even talking about doing more to engage members has had repercussions. After Marcuz read Jane McAlevey’s organizing guide 

No Shortcuts

, he brought up the possibility of opening up bargaining to his union rep. A few days later, he was removed from his position as steward, and was told that more “loyalty” was expected from him. 




Marcuz and his co-workers encountered similar resistance when they collected 300 petition signatures for Zoom access to union meetings, which are only held in-person at the union office in Roseville—a several-hour drive for many members of the local, which is spread out across 40 counties. The same happened when they organized bowling socials.




During their campaign, union staff representatives have allegedly told members that it’s illegal to wear At What Cost buttons or to provide contact information to the slate. At a Safeway store in Turlock, a rep physically pulled a member away from speaking to Marcuz. 




“Workers face exploitation through contract violations, wage theft, and unsafe staffing and working conditions,” Marcuz said. “We could organize against these issues, but our leadership seems more interested in collaborating with the corporations creating these conditions than with the members who pay their salaries.”




In early November, members of the slate will be working to collect 443 petition signatures—2 percent of active members—to get on the ballot and force the first competitive election in memory.

author: Natascha Elena Uhlmann
title: Mexico Volkswagen Workers Could Soon Strike
content:
In Mexico, at the world’s largest Volkswagen facility outside of Germany, workers are weighing the risks of a possible strike.




The 6,500 workers build the Jetta, Tiguan, and Taos at the company’s Puebla plant. Their union, SITIAVW, is one of Mexico’s most storied independent unions, and is in the midst of the plant’s annual wage reopener negotiations.




Days before the strike deadline of October 22, the company presented two proposals—offering raises of 7.98 percent and 7.95 percent for a one-year duration—which were rejected by the union. Soon afterwards, the company presented another offer: an 8.24 percent increase, of which 3.59 percent is a one-time payment of 12,000 pesos, equivalent to about $641 U.S. The deal would maintain the yearly salary reopener, a cycle the company had tried to lengthen in previous offers. Workers will vote on the offer on October 28, and could strike the next day if a deal is not reached. 




On October 15, workers voted down an offer that  would have provided a 13 percent combined increase to wages and benefits over the next two years. The vote was 3,135 against and 2,452 for. 




A month earlier, workers had overwhelmingly voted down the previous offer of a 10 percent combined increase. (The union had been pushing for a 17 percent increase earlier in negotiations.) Days before that first agreement was put to a vote, Volkswagen cut one of three shifts in a segment of the plant that produces the Jetta and the Tiguan. About 

800 workers

 lost their jobs, 

El Financiero

 reported.




Although the union announced that 611 of the workers—those who did not sign voluntary separation agreements—would be eligible for reinstatement when Volkswagen begins production of its Golf compact car at the Puebla facility next April, the damage was done. 5,925 of the company’s 6,440 eligible voters participated in the ratification vote: of them, 

73 percent voted to reject the offer

, in what SITIAVW advisor Willebaldo Gómez Zuppa characterized as an expression of anger at the firings. The deal would have also 

pushed the next wage reopener

 to 18 months out instead of the yearly cycle, angering workers.




‘NOT AT OUR EXPENSE’




Workers were also frustrated with the company’s efforts to put off their next wage reopener for 18 months rather than a year. The second offer would have pushed the wage reopener out even further, to two years.




“We are not blind to the delicate crisis facing the German automotive industry, nor are we ignoring the global financial challenges Volkswagen cites,” the union 

said

 in a statement in September after workers voted down the first offer. “But let it be heard loud and clear, all the way to Wolfsburg: corporate crises will not be resolved at the expense of the sweat, the rights, and the future of the Mexican working class.”




Volkswagen did not respond to requests for comment. In a statement sent to 

La Jornada de Oriente

, VW 

said

, "We respect the result of the vote... and at the same time, express our deep worry and disappointment. This agreement represents the greatest viable offer from the company, given current conditions.” 




GLOBAL LAYOFFS




In September, VW announced plans to eliminate 

50,000 jobs

 globally by 2030, alongside another 50,000 already anticipated cuts—together representing the largest culling of jobs ever by a single automaker.




The company noted in September that its European factories have the capacity to produce 

500,000 more vehicles per year

 than it can sell. The industry faces 

“enormous pressure”

 due to low cost electric vehicles produced in China, Volkswagen's CEO Oliver ​Blume said at the Paris Motor Show in October.  Its restructuring plan calls for eliminating half the models it produces (the less profitable half).




IG Metall, which represents 120,000 Volkswagen workers in Germany and sits on the company’s supervisory board, agreed to accept the closure of four German plants between 2031 and 2034, telling the 

Guardian

 that both labor and management had made concessions to stave off “a dangerous escalation of the conflict.”




Workers at VW's only U.S. assembly plant, in Chattanooga, Tennessee, joined the United Auto Workers in 2024 after years of trying, and ratified their first contract earlier this year. So far the cuts have not affected them.




It remains unclear how many more cuts are expected in Puebla. Since 2012, the plant has cut its workforce by 36 percent, 

Milenio reported

, but it remains one of the largest employers in the state of Puebla today.




About 6,500 production workers are directly employed at the plant, which produces vehicles largely for export to the United States. Some 39,000 more work in the auto supply chain across the state, including 3,500 at the local Audi plant, and thousands more in the parts sector, 

producing seats, motor components, and electronics

.




The offer that workers voted down in October included a guarantee that the 611 members laid off in September would be rehired in the future, and guaranteed jobs for the current workforce.




AUTO STRIKES RARE




Unlike in the U.S., where companies can try to continue operations during a strike by using managers and hiring replacement workers, under Mexican labor law, companies must cease all production at a struck plant. That gives Mexican unions tremendous potential power. 




Yet strikes in the country’s auto industry, the world’s seventh-largest, have been exceedingly rare in recent decades, with most of the industry’s contracts held by employer-friendly “protection unions” who have been a key partner in Mexico’s low-wage development model. SITIAVW, one of the few independent unions, has won the highest wages in the industry.




In this case, however, some analysts have speculated that the company may welcome a strike.




In Mexico, employers must provide a justification to the government for laying off workers. Among those justifications can be losses incurred due to a strike, said SITIAVW adviser Willebaldo Gomez Zuppa: “It opens the door before the government to say, ‘That’s why I have to fire so many people.’”




“It’s not hard to go out on strike,” said Hugo Tlalpan, SITIAVW’s General Secretary. “The hard thing is ending it.”




ONE MINUTE LATE




The Puebla plant has been in operation since 1967. In the plant’s early days, workers were affiliated with the Confederation of Mexican Workers, or CTM, a labor confederation known for imposing pro-employer “protection contracts” on workers. But in 1972, workers split off from the CTM and formed the independent SITIAVW. Since then, the plant has seen a number of strikes and workplace actions—and nearly as many efforts from Mexico’s halls of power to subvert them. 




In 1992, 

14,500 workers at the Puebla facility struck

 to expel their union leadership that some workers felt was complicit in negotiating an employer-friendly contract. With the blessing of the Secretary of Labor, the company 

 locked them out,

 then fired them. About 10,000 were rehired a day later, but under an agreement that 

imposed

 higher productivity targets, flexible scheduling, and a reduction in benefits.




In 2000, workers struck again, and once more their strike was 

quashed

 with support of Mexico’s labor authorities. Because workers went out on strike at 11:01 a.m. instead of exactly at 11, their stated strike deadline, the Federal Arbitration Board deemed their strike invalid. (They struck a year later and clinched 

 14.7 percent raises

.) 




The union is carefully weighing its options in this round of negotiations; so far, SITIAVW has extended its strike deadline 

four times.

 Most recently, just two days before the September 17 strike deadline, the union extended the deadline to Friday, October 2. 




“This is an attack on one of the most robust collective bargaining agreements [in the country],” Gomez Zuppa said. What happens next will have repercussions for autoworkers throughout Mexico and Volkswagen workers across the world.

author: Jenny Brown
title: Tampa TSA Union Averted   Privatization Disaster
content:
TSA agents noticed something was up. “We started seeing people around the airport that you wouldn’t normally see, people in suits,” said Mark Harris, Transportation Security Officer and union steward in Tampa, Florida.  




That’s when he realized the airport was a target for the TSA privatization program he had been reading about—the $13 billion Gold+ program. Harris, and his union Government Employees (AFGE) Local 556, swung into action. 




Transportation Security Administration workers have been winning battles lately. Twice in two years the Trump administration has tried to cancel their union contract, and twice it has been stopped by the courts. Now things are mostly back to normal, with the contract in force and grievances being processed.




But Gold+ would undermine the union by outsourcing TSO jobs to private companies. As the dimensions of the plan became clear, Harris said his co-workers “felt like they had been kicked in the gut. You know, everything that they had worked for, their federal pension, careers, everything.”




Tampa is a model airport that consistently ranks at the top in customer satisfaction. That’s why TSA picked it for the Gold+ privatization effort, Harris said. “They don’t want to give it to a poor airport or a failing airport. That would be disastrous for TSA, right?”

author: Caitlyn Clark
title: Interview: How We Beat Back Nonunion Subcontracting at Kroger
content:
After more than six months fighting against Kroger’s use of non-union subcontractors, members of Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 700 in Indiana won a 

victory

 in August, when Kroger announced it would be ending the Retail Odyssey direct store delivery (DSD) program entirely.




This means more hours for union members—thanks to those who organized to enforce the contract, file grievances, and educate their co-workers. In this interview conducted by Caitlyn Clark of the reform group Essential Workers for Democracy, shop stewards Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson explain how they did it.




Essential Workers for Democracy: What is Retail Odyssey and why is it a problem? 




Andrea Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey is a nonunion third-party contractor that solely services Kroger stores. Normally RO does things like rearranging a store layout or auditing whether products are displayed the way the brand wants.




A few months ago, the Kroger Central Division here in Indiana developed a new program utilizing RO employees to stock direct store delivery vendor items on weekends. [

DSD items are delivered straight to the store by the supplier, rather than coming through a Kroger warehouse.

]




Why is this a problem? Kroger has employees who need hours. This isn't “extra help.” Kroger wants to phase nonunion third parties into the stores to cut hours of its union employees. If we don't speak up, it will only get worse. We’ve seen this happen already with cut fruit vendors, outdoor floral products, floor cleaning, and gift cards, just to name a few. 




How did you and your co-workers start taking on Retail Odyssey?

 




Reynolds:

 We immediately started gathering as much accurate information as we could and passing it along to our co-workers. We shared information in our Facebook group and we shared flyers with our co-workers.




We wanted them to know why this was a problem and what they could do about it. The company wants us to think that third parties are there to make our jobs easier. But time and time again, we see our hours cut and wonder why. 




We also passed along the feedback of our vendors. Their products were being damaged, mixed with other vendors, and stocked incorrectly. 




Kristen Jackson:

 Although in the pharmacy, I am not as impacted, my union brothers and sisters are. As a steward, I try my best to let others know what is wrong with RO taking our work.




I walked around and talked to my co-workers about what the RO workers were allowed to stock. I told them if they saw them, to please take pictures, talk to the RO workers, and be nice.













By having a standardized report form, members could make sure grievances were airtight.










How did you collect information to file grievances? How did you make sure grievances got filed and processed?




Reynolds:

 Retail Odyssey was scheduled to work Friday through Sunday, noon to 6 p.m. I had a lot of conversations with members I knew were normally there during those hours.




I instructed them to take photos, make note of the day, time, duration of stocking, what non-vendor products were stocked, and anyone who witnessed it. We had them send this info to our stewards or trusted employees who could contact our union rep.




Every week after the grievance was filed, we messaged our reps asking for status of the grievance. We didn't want it to fall through the cracks.




Jackson:

 I just went up to the RO workers, introduced myself as a steward, and let them know I would be taking pictures of them and why. I explained, “I'm not against you having a job. I'm here to document Kroger violating our contract.”




The RO workers were understanding, and would tell me that the manager told them to stock our product and let me file the grievances. The RO worker at my store location would tell me exactly what he stocked, so I could file the grievances effectively. We filed three grievances at my location. 




What advice would you give to anyone dealing with non-union subcontracting?




Reynolds:

 Document, document, document! You need to prove there was a contract violation.




Talk with your co-workers about how to document. Contact your rep. Don't hesitate to ask for help from a steward or a trusted member.




You have power in your numbers. The more members speaking up, the better! We filed so many grievances in six months that the third-party DSD program has officially ended. When we fight, we win. 			




Andrea Reynolds and Kristen Jackson are UFCW Local 700 shop stewards in Kokomo and Zionsville, Indiana. Caitlyn Clark is the director of Essential Workers for Democracy.

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Labor Goes on Election Defense
content:
New York City unions representing 1 million members launched a new coalition October 15 to defend the right to vote ahead of the midterm elections November 3. A thousand members rallied outside the city’s main post office, pledging to mobilize the labor movement to defend the elections from Trump administration interference. 




The throng included large contingents from Laborers Locals 78 and 79, the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, building services and airport workers from SEIU 32BJ, and health care workers from 1199SEIU. There were also union telecom workers, nurses, stagehands, municipal workers, retail workers, postal workers, electricians, grocery workers, office workers, and painters. 




The NYC Central Labor Council initiative, called “Our Voice, Our Vote, Our Democracy,” aims to turn out union members and their communities to protest peacefully and to document intimidation of voters. It was announced just ahead of October 17, when the No Kings coalition held 3,000 events nationwide to promote early voting.




“We are demanding democratic and fair elections,” said SEIU 32BJ President Manny Pastreich in a statement to 

Labor Notes

. “In anticipation of possible election sabotage, unions have hosted dozens of know-your-rights trainings, have organized hundreds of poll-watchers, and have created rapid-response networks.”

author: Unknown
title: Book Review: Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line
content:
Union strength or weakness is often seen only through the light of a strike or lockout. Phil Cohen’s memoir, 

Maximum Leverage: From the Street to the Picket Line

, tells a different story. Union building is on-going, from organizing to win a first contract, to maintaining and strengthening that contract over time, from grievance handling to arbitration, from safety and health to pension rights. And in every situation there is a need to build membership participation, develop and support local leadership, strengthen mutual support, ensure understanding of rights, understanding of power and how to wield it (or lose it). 




Cohen demonstrates as much as he explains how every aspect of the above is at the heart of a union’s ability to improve conditions on the job, improve pay and benefits, and ultimately be able to win on the picket line if it comes to that.




A chapter recalling fighting back against a union-busting attorney during bargaining is emblematic. BTR Sealing Systems in Reidsville, North Carolina—a factory making wiper blades for auto companies—negotiated a first contract with workers after the plant was organized in 1995. Frequent grievances and conflicts with supervisors were part of the reality where both workers and frontline supervisors were unfamiliar with negotiating day-to-day disputes via a contract. title: Trabajadores de la salud de Iowa exigen el regreso de una compañera deportada
content:
Fatou Traore se dirigía a su trabajo como personal de limpieza en los Hospitales y Clínicas de la Universidad de Iowa (UIHC) en la mañana del jueves 24 de septiembre, cuando agentes de ICE la detuvieron. 




A pesar de tener estatus migratorio legal en Estados Unidos, y sin antecedentes penales, fue deportada a Sierra Leone—un lugar con el que no tiene ningún vínculo—el 12 de octubre. Traore es una querida integrante de la comunidad de Iowa City, y del Local 12 del Consejo 61 de AFSCME. También es madre de cuatro hijos, el menor de los cuales tiene solo tres años. 




Cuando aprendí que fue detenida en Septiembre, me indignó que ICE se había llevado a alguien del mero hospital donde yo trabajaba. Muchos de los trabajadores en el hospital no sabían de su detención, o temían alzar la voz. Les escribí a todos los flebotomistas con los que había trabajado en la sede principal; algunos quienes también habían sido personal de limpieza en algún momento, y habían trabajado con Fatou.

author: Unknown
title: Iowa Hospital Workers Demand Return of Deported Co-Worker
content:
Fatou Traore was on her way to work as a custodian at the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics (UIHC) on the morning of Thursday, September 24, when ICE agents detained her. 




Despite having legal immigration status in the United States and no criminal record, she was deported to Sierra Leone (a place she has no connection to) on October 12. Traore is a beloved member of the Iowa City community and of AFSCME Council 61, Local 12. She is also the mother of four children, the youngest of whom is three years old.




When I first heard the news of her September detention, I was upset that ICE had taken someone from the very hospital where I worked. Many of the workers at the hospital weren’t aware of her detention or were afraid to speak up. I wrote to all of the inpatient phlebotomists I used to work with at main campus, some of whom had also been custodians and worked with Fatou. 




I wrote an opinion letter for a local paper, 

Little Village

. I helped spread the word to raise awareness of her detention across community networks, from my supervisors and senior administration at UIHC, to the soccer team that my son plays on, to the yoga community I belong to, to my own family and their church communities, to the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, which I graduated from in 2022—to every person that I knew.

author: Luis Feliz Leon, Jane Slaughter
title: UAW President Shawn Fain Wins Reelection Victory
content:
United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain has won a second four-year term, winning 68 percent of the vote in 

member balloting

 for the union’s top officers. 




The election was a 

referendum on the new fighting direction

 Fain has taken the union by leading 2023’s 

Stand-Up Strike

 against the Big 3 automakers, other 

bold

 

contract

 fights, and new organizing campaigns.




It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021.




According to unofficial tallies posted online, Fain won more than two-thirds of the vote, against five opponents. His nearest competitor, incumbent vice president Rich Boyer, had 14 percent. Challenged ballots are still to be counted, and the election results are yet to be officially certified.




Fain is running as part of the 

United UAW

 slate. His slate-mate for secretary-treasurer, Brandon Campbell, has also garnered two-thirds, against two rivals including incumbent Margaret Mock. 




The slate’s candidates for the three vice president spots were also elected with 20-25 percent each in a field of 11 candidates. (VP candidates need 16.7 percent to win.) The slate has also won all the regional director races it contested.

title: UAW President Shawn Fain Nears Reelection Victory
content:
United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain looks poised to win a second four-year term, with an overwhelming lead in 

member balloting

 for the union’s top officers. 




The election was a 

referendum on the new fighting direction

 Fain has taken the union by leading 2023’s 

Stand-Up Strike

 against the Big 3 automakers, other 

bold

 

contract

 fights, and new organizing campaigns.




It marks the second time members have voted for their top officers in the union’s 91 years. UAW members voted to switch to a one-member-one-vote system in December 2021.




With votes in eight of the union’s nine regions counted as of Friday morning, Fain had more than two-thirds of the vote, against five opponents. His nearest competitor, incumbent vice president Rich Boyer, had 14 percent.




Fain is running as part of the 

United UAW

 slate. His slate-mate for secretary-treasurer, Brandon Campbell, has also garnered two-thirds, against two rivals including incumbent Margaret Mock. 




The slate’s candidates for the three vice president spots appeared on track to be elected with 19-25 percent each in a field of 11 candidates. (VP candidates need 16.7 percent to win.) The slate has also won all the regional director races counted thus far that it contested.

title: Palestinian Arts Workers Call for Solidarity
content:
Palestinian cultural workers living through apartheid, occupation, and genocide are 

calling for solidarity

Not every artist has as large a platform as rapper Macklemore, children’s TV star Miss Rachel, or country singer Zach Bryan—who wore a “Free Palestine” shirt last weekend while playing a packed show at the same stadium where billionaire Robert Kraft had barred Macklemore for saying those words—but there’s plenty that artists and art workers can do to end complicity in Israel’s ongoing atrocities.




We as Palestinians have long decried Israel’s war crimes and crimes against humanity. Now the 

Palestinian Performing Arts Network

 (PPAN), representing hundreds of Palestinian dancers, actors, musicians, playwrights, and circus performers, has 

outlined

author: Luis Feliz Leon
title: Amazon Package Drivers Rev Up Organizing to Become Direct Employees
content:
The workers who wear Amazon vests and drive vans with the company’s logo aren’t legally employed by Amazon. But that could change in New York City, under legislation that Teamsters and Amazon workers alongside the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are organizing to pass. 




The Delivery Protection Act would require Amazon, alongside FedEx and other companies, to directly employ drivers rather than rely on third-party subcontractors. It would also establish safety, training, and labor standards for delivery drivers. 




As of October 3, workers and allies had knocked on 11,446 doors across the Bronx, Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Staten Island, according to the Teamsters. 




Across the country, 4,500 tiny companies act as Amazon’s delivery service partners (DSPs)—meaning these contractors are the nominal employers, even while the logistics giant retains control.




“For years, Amazon has relied on a convoluted subcontracting system that denies last-mile drivers the protections other workers get, while maintaining extraordinary control over their schedules, workloads, and uniforms,” said Julie Su, New York City’s deputy mayor for economic justice, in a statement. 




Treating DSP delivery drivers as Amazon’s direct employees would make the company responsible for wage and safety protections and other legal liabilities. A similar bill is under consideration in Chicago.

title: Film Review: A Portrait of How Workers Build a Strike
content:
“Who Moves America” is touring the U.S., with upcoming screenings across the West Coast, Northeast, and South. See when it’s coming to your town, or request a screening, 

here

.




In the new documentary 

“Who Moves America,”

 filmmaker Yael Bridge offers a window into the working-class culture of one of the country’s largest unions, the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, at United Parcel Service (UPS) in 2023.




It’s a rare and moving portrait of a massive, diverse group of workers building themselves into a fighting force, who then must wrestle with a different version of victory than they expected.


We watch as 340,000 Teamsters gear up for a potential strike against package giant United Parcel Service, the largest private-sector union contract in North America. Behind the wheel in brown trucks and along conveyor belts in warehouses, their working conditions are grueling and dangerous: at the time, two drivers had died in the past year from sweltering heat.




If they strike, their market leverage from moving 6 percent of the country’s gross domestic product means they can cripple the company’s profits and send shock waves across the economy.

title: How Unions Can Reverse Privatization of Medicaid and Why It Matters
content:
The following was adapted from a March 2026 speech that Rose Roach, National Coordinator for the Labor Campaign for Single Payer, gave to the Minnesota AFL-CIO.




In July 2025, President Trump signed HR1 into law, inflicting a trillion dollars of federal cuts on our nation’s lifesaving state-based Medicaid programs. Meanwhile, Congress allowed the tax credits available for people enrolled in Affordable Care Act (ACA) insurance exchanges to expire. 




These cuts impact all of us, even those with union-negotiated health care plans. That’s because when emergency rooms and hospitals have more uninsured patients, they provide more uncompensated care. To cover that loss, providers increase prices, and insurance companies in turn increase premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who are still insured. 




Union members who are insured through their employers are already seeing their exorbitant health insurance premiums rise to some of the highest levels we’ve seen in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Medicare Advantage plans (privatized, for-profit insurance) serving retirees are closing shop or increasing premiums while cutting benefits. Those on a Medicare supplemental or Medigap plan are seeing hefty premium increases as well.
